title: Vijay Singh: 30 years since racially bullied Manchester teen died

input.evidence_text: Vijay Singh: 30 years since racially bullied Manchester teen died - BBC News Image source, Preet Kaur Image caption, Vijay Singh was 13 when he died By Georgie Docker and Haider Saleem , Reporting from North West Published 53 minutes ago Warning: This article contains details which some may find distressing "Monday: My money was taken. "Tuesday: Names called. "Wednesday: My uniform torn. "Thursday: My body pouring with blood. "Friday: It's ended. Saturday: Freedom." This was the last entry made by 13-year-old Manchester schoolboy Vijay Singh in his journal before his death on Saturday 12 October, 1996. Described as a "caring" older brother, the avid Manchester United fan was said to have been a "confident" and "popular" boy until he was targeted by racist bullies. His family were not aware of this abuse until after his death. A coroner recorded an open verdict at Vijay's inquest but his family believe he took his own life. Vijay's little sister Preet Kaur is now 34. She spoke to the BBC on the 30th anniversary of his death, both to tell her brother's story and to speak out against bullying and racism. Image source, Preet Kaur Image caption, As well as his sister Preet (pictured here standing in front of him), Vijay had five brothers "It has been 30 years since Vijay's death," Preet said. "I guess we learn to live with that but we don't forget the pain and the hurt that is caused over the years." Preet was only four when she lost him. Being so young, she said her memories of him had largely been influenced by watching home videos. "Vijay was very, very protective and caring of myself and our siblings," she said. Vijay played football at his school in Stretford and was a popular member of the local Sikh community. "He was a keen footballer and a very avid fan of Mancheste

title: Rochdale school with over 1,000 pupils evacuated over hoax bomb threat

input.lead: Police say a bomb threat which was called into St Cuthbert's Roman Catholic High School was a "hoax"
input.summary: Police say a bomb threat which was called into St Cuthbert's Roman Catholic High School was a "hoax"
input.evidence_text: Rochdale school with over 1,000 pupils evacuated over hoax bomb threat - BBC News Image caption, St Cuthbert's Roman Catholic High School was put into lockdown by school staff after the bomb threat By Stewart Whittingham North West Published 16 October 2026 A school of more than 1,000 pupils was evacuated after a hoax bomb threat was made. St Cuthbert's Roman Catholic High School was put into lockdown after the bomb call at 08:55 BST and staff dialled 999. Greater Manchester Police (GMP) said it investigated but found it was a hoax. The school, which has more than 1,100 pupils, has been closed for the day. GMP said it was investigating. A GMP spokesman said: "The school implemented a lockdown in response to a suspicious call. "Officers attended and carried out an assessment which indicated that the call was a likely hoax. "Officers are investigating the circumstances of the call." The trust which runs the school, St Teresa of Calcutta Catholic Academy Trust, said "parents and carers were notified immediately that their children had been removed to a safe distance and there was no threat or danger to anyone present". 'False rumours' A statement on Facebook added: "We would like to assure everyone within the St Cuthbert's School community that the safety and wellbeing of our children remains our absolute priority." The trust urged people to "avoid speculation on social media - particularly regarding false rumours, such as any referring to intruders or weapons being present on school premises". It added: "The current expectation is that the school will be open as normal on Monday 19 October and further details will be shared when appropriate." Earlier this year, staff at St Cuthbert's held a series of strikes over claims of "violent and abusive behaviour from some pupils".

title: Nurse's death after misdiagnosed condition needless, family says

input.lead: Paula Ivers went to hospital complaining of chest pain but was told it was acid reflux and sent home
input.summary: Paula Ivers went to hospital complaining of chest pain but was told it was acid reflux and sent home
input.evidence_text: Nurse's death after misdiagnosed condition needless, family says - BBC News Image source, Family photo Image caption, Paula Ivers was found collapsed at home by her nine-year-old daughter By Stewart Whittingham North West Published 16 October 2026 The family of a nurse who died just days after her life-threatening heart condition was misdiagnosed have said her "needless" death has left them "devastated". Paula Ivers went to Tameside General Hospital with chest pain but was sent home after being told it was acid reflux, her inquest heard. The 47-year-old children's nurse died three days later at her home in Denton, Tameside, in March 2024. A coroner concluded the death was contributed to by neglect. Her sister Lesley Ivers said she "received poor care from the NHS when she needed it most". "We are devastated to have lost her," the 51-year-old said. "Our family will never be the same." She said her niece "lost her mother at such a young age". "She was just nine when her mum died and was home alone with her at the time. "Paula's death has left a huge void in our family and the pain of losing her is still as raw today as it was when she needlessly passed away. "We feel very disappointed in the NHS." The mother-of-one went to the A&E department at the hospital in Ashton-under-Lyne in severe pain on 8 March 2024. Her inquest heard she had gastroesophageal reflux disease and was sent home with a prescription for indigestion medication. Image source, Family handout Image caption, The mother-of-one, right, died three days after being sent home from hospital Stockport Coroner's Court heard a tear in her aorta - the main artery of the body - resulted in a cardiac arrest. Her father had died of a heart-related issue in his 40s, indicating a history in the family, the inquest heard.

title: Samurai sword, £70k cash and gun seized in Manchester drug raids

input.summary: Four men were arrested and five others later came forward themselves, Greater Manchester Police say
input.evidence_text: Samurai sword, £70k cash and gun seized in Manchester drug raids - BBC News Image source, GMP Image caption, A viable semi-automatic gun was found during the police raids across Manchester, police say Published 16 October 2026 Police have seized a samurai sword and a semi-automatic gun along with £70,000 in cash after a series of drug raids. Cocaine and MDMA were also found alongside the firearm and ammunition, Greater Manchester Police (GMP) said. GMP said four men, in their 20s and 30s, were arrested and five more later came forward themselves. All nine have now been released on bail pending further inquiries. Image source, GMP Image caption, Drugs including MDMA and cocaine were found in the raids Armed police then raided eight properties in Moss Side, Levenshulme, Moston, and Harpurhey. Det Cons Katie Havens said the raids had "prevented dangerous weapons and illegal drugs from reaching our streets". They toiled over six years to create the foundation of a magnificent feat of engineering - the Manchester Ship Canal It opened for traffic from January 1, 1894. It cost more than £15m, equivalent today to £2.1bn. The 36 miles waterway from Salford to the Irish Sea was forged by labourers from Ireland, Scotland, Wales, and south west England as well as the streets of Manchester and Salford As they grafted to provide for their families back home hundreds lost their lives in landslides and accidents But one result of their sacrifice was "Manchester Docks", which was actually in Salford. Mr Mullins was trapped under the car while his damaged bike was left in the road

Sue Hall worked for two years in what was for a time the tallest building in the country, from the day Born in a working class Collyhurst pub – The Milan – in the latter years of WWII, Sue and female friends of her upbringing weren’t expected to get fancy office jobs. But at just 15 she joined the Co-operative Insurance Society (CIS). Her first setup was a tall wooden stool and de As the times changed, 34 out of 35 girls from her Moston Lane Secondary class joined the CIS, and at lunch some of them would walk to the shops for sweets or crisps surrounded by smog so thick that she couldn’t see the friend by her side But it was a good employer with lots of prospects, so she hung around. Four years later and the city air had cleaned up enough for her to walk south to Shudehill and crane her neck up at the monolith of glass that was soon to be her next place of work: Manchester’s first skyscrap Like the intrepid journalist I am, I ask Sue what sort of fashion people wore then. She seems unsure of how to answer so she tells me “just normal clothes”. Her daughter Lynda is on hand beside Sue in her plush-cushioned tall-back arm chair. Lynda shows me a picture of Sue and he Opened in 1962, the CIS Tower was a testament to Manchester's ambitions in the new age of post-war Americanism: cars everywhere and buildings ever higher. title: Royton Library finds a new temporary home as essential repair works progress

input.lead: The library will reopen at a temporary location from Monday 19 October, ensuring residents can continue to access book lending services in their community
input.summary: The library will reopen at a temporary location from Monday 19 October, ensuring residents can continue to access book lending services in their community
input.evidence_text: The library will reopen at a temporary location from Monday 19 October, ensuring residents can continue to access book lending services in their community The temporary library will operate from Downey House on Church Street, Royton, OL2 5JS, the historic former home of the Cooper family of cotton manufacturers and now home to St Paul's Parish Centre The move follows the temporary closure of Royton Library on Rochdale Road to allow investigations and repairs to flooring within the building. The works are essential to ensure library remains a safe, welcoming and accessible space for the future The temporary Royton Library service at Downey House will be open 9am to 5pm on Monday and Saturday at 9.30am to 1pm. The temporary library will provide a book lending service, with a collection of popular titles for both adults and children available to borrow Subnum Hariff-Khan, Head of Heritage, Libraries and Arts for Oldham Council, said: "We know how important Royton Library is to local residents and we're pleased to be able to continue delivering a library service within the community while these essential repairs take place "We'd like to thank customers for their patience and understanding while these essential works are carried out to secure the future of this important library building."

More capital is being concentrated in fewer companies while the market for exits remains difficult Financial news recently added another dimension to that discussion. AI-related shares fell last week after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for a slower approach to the development of increasingly capable AI models. Nvidia finished the day down 3.4%, SoftBank fell 10.7% in Tokyo Additionally, the Bank of England is predicted to increase interest rates later this year, which could affect the North West's tech funding landscape by raising the cost of capital across the board, compressing valuations, pushing investors toward profitability over growth-at-all The British Business Bank's 2026 Small Business Equity Tracker found that equity investment into UK smaller businesses fell 4% to £12.3bn in 2025. Seed deal numbers fell 27% and venture deals fell 13%. AI companies attracted 44% of all investment into smaller businesses while the Beauhurst recorded £14.4bn of UK equity investment across 2,799 deals in the first half of 2026 but three AI companies accounted for 29% of all the capital raised. Those very large rounds can make the overall market look stronger than it feels to businesses raising at seed or Ser Beauhurst's analysis shows that UK equity investment more than doubled between 2017 and 2021 to £32.2bn while annual exits remained at around 400 to 500. input.evidence_text: In 1965, The Sunday Times Magazine sent photojournalist John Bulmer north to document the region at a time when it was defined by industrial decline. But the images he returned with told a more complex story: shot in colour, they showed humanity and dignity alongside the hardship Sixty years later, photographer Simon Hill has retraced that journey. The conversation between their two bodies of work, now showing together at Jodrell Bank, builds a portrait of how much has changed since then and how much remains While Bulmer visited 16 locations across the North, Hill travelled to more than 50. From late 2024 to mid 2026 he crossed the historic seven counties from Newcastle to Liverpool, visiting former mining communities, coastal towns, city centres, remote landscapes, and the motorways In homage to Bulmer’s pioneering use of colour, much of Hill’s work was shot on Harman Phoenix 200, a contemporary colour film made in the North, and known for its unpredictable, textured qualities Bulmer’s North captured communities facing uncertain futures as the industries that defined them began to disappear. Hill’s is post-industrial, more diverse and still evolving. Former centres of heavy industry have become sites of cultural reinvention and technological growth. Bu Jodrell Bank feels a particularly fitting setting for work that’s fundamentally about time, distance and how we measure change. title: Bolton Car Boot Sale

input.lead: Bolton Car Boot Sale at Bolton Car Boot Sale
input.summary: Bolton Car Boot Sale is one of the North West's biggest weekly boot sales, held in the hardstanding car park of the Macron Stadium (formerly Reebok), Burnden Way, Horwich, Bolton BL6 6JW. It runs every Sunday from February right through to December, drawing over 300 sellers and t
input.evidence_text: Bolton Car Boot Sale is one of the North West's biggest weekly boot sales, held in the hardstanding car park of the Macron Stadium (formerly Reebok), Burnden Way, Horwich, Bolton BL6 6JW. It runs every Sunday from February right through to December, drawing over 300 sellers and thousands of bargain hunters each week. Sellers can arrive and set up from 6:00 AM, with buyers welcomed in from 7:00 AM. Entry costs just £1 per car for buyers. Pitches for sellers are £14 for a car, £20 for a van and £3 for a trailer, with regular and corner pitches available on request. Bring exact change to keep the queue moving, and call organiser Andrew on 07470784644 for more details. Expect hundreds of stalls across the concrete hardstanding pitches, so it goes ahead in most weather. On-site you'll find a 5-star catering service, doughnuts and coffee, ice cream and desserts, a meat auction, fresh fruit and veg, plants, and retro sweet stalls. The sale is dog-friendly, has male and female toilets, ample parking, and kids' rides and bouncy castles to keep little ones entertained. Last confirmed: 10 September 2026 Event date: 2026-10-18 Venue: Bolton Car Boot Sale Price: £1 Status: https://schema.org/EventScheduled
